JUL 15 2026

How We Built Our Knowledge Base
ISAAC TAI
DANIEL KIM
MIKE GAO

Employees ask our internal knowledge base more than 15,000 questions every day. It's become one of the most widely adopted internal tools at the company since launching 3 months ago. Used by humans, automations and agents.

At Cerebras, our teams work across data center operations, chip design, hardware, training, inference, cloud platform, and more. With hundreds of new employees joining every year, our communication channels were filling up with the same questions:

“Where can I find X?”
“Who is the expert in Y?”
“What is Z?”

We built Cerebras Knowledge to help people connect people and systems to useful information.

Meeting data where it lives

Finding information inside an organization is hard. The data is scattered across tools, and every quarter or so someone proposes the same brilliant fix: let’s record everything in one platform so that all information is in a single place. The dream of a single source of truth, of course, rarely works in practice.

Information is generated wherever it is convenient and ergonomic: suggested edits in a document, threads in Slack, code references in GitHub, and status metadata in Jira. These platforms are tailor-made for their specific domains, optimized through years of product engineering and analytics. Discussing a pull request in Google Docs would be a terrible experience.

So we set out to design a system that required minimal change to existing behavior. On the data collection side, this meant extracting data from each platform directly.

Anatomy of a knowledge base

Our knowledge base provides three things:

A platform for collecting and storing internal data.
A platform for querying that data.
A layer that enforces authentication and authorization, with auditing and analytics.

At the core is a single Postgres table that holds embeddings, raw summaries, and metadata from many sources. The system continually ingests data from across the company and maintains a query-ready datastore.

We wanted a data interface that was simple but could work with most forms of data. We also wanted other developers at Cerebras to be able to build custom connectors. The result is deliberately simple: every source, from Slack threads to netlists, lands in the same embeddings table, and anything in that table is immediately queryable through the same interface:

Each data source defines what the data is, how to connect to it, and how often it should be fetched. Each resulting embedding row follows the same interface regardless of whether it came from Slack, a code repository, a document system, or a custom database.

Slack

Slack was the most important data source we needed to design for. It is where the most up-to-date engineering discussions happen across the company.

How we process unstructured Slack conversations

We initially tested whether simple embeddings over raw text performed well enough. We quickly realized that vector search alone was insufficient for matching all relevant data.

Slack messages present several challenges:

Information density varies enormously: “hey yeah sure mike” and a detailed kernel explanation are both messages.
Message lengths vary, and shorter messages frequently beat longer, more detailed messages in cosine similarity.
The meaning of a message often depends on the surrounding conversation.

We needed a hybrid approach. We built Slack ingestion so every thread is retrievable through several search techniques at once, where each technique makes up for the weaknesses of the others:

Full-text search catches the exact tokens that embeddings blur together: error strings, flag names, host names. When an engineer pastes a literal error message, an exact lexical match is almost always the best evidence, and no amount of semantic similarity should outrank it.
Embedding search catches paraphrase. The person asking “restore hangs after manifest load” and the person who answered “checkpoint stalls on the NFS mount” may never share vocabulary. Vector similarity is what connects a question to an answer written in different words.(1)
Inverse document frequency separates signal from filler. A short message built around rare tokens, such as an obscure config flag, deserves to rank. “sounds good, thanks!” sits close to many queries in embedding space but scores near zero once term rarity is taken into account.
Age decay encodes that Slack answers expire. Two threads can answer the same question, and the one from six months ago may describe infrastructure that no longer exists. When relevance is otherwise equal, the newer thread wins.

No single scorer is trusted on its own. Each technique produces its own ranked view of the same corpus, and those views are fused at query time (see Reranking).

Socket Mode

To collect data in real time, we installed a Slack bot into our workspace and ran it in Socket Mode. Slack pushes every message event to us over a persistent WebSocket, so we get real-time updates without polling the Web API and burning through its rate limits.

When an event arrives, we immediately acknowledge it, deduplicate it using the stable event ID, and mark the message for the ingest consumer.

The ingest consumer does not save a new message in isolation. It resolves the thread that the message belongs to and re-fetches the entire conversation, including the parent and every reply, from the Slack API. It then writes the whole thread back as one row. A reply to an existing thread therefore re-pulls the parent and all siblings, so the stored content, participant list, and last-activity timestamp always reflect the complete conversation.

Every Slack channel in our system has its own data source. This provides fine-grained tuning for data freshness. A team may choose to ingest a busy incident channel more frequently, for example.

Threads and messages

Raw Slack text is keyword-searchable as soon as it lands because we maintain a Postgres full-text (GIN) index over the raw content. To enable useful vector search, however, we do some additional processing.(8)

We embed these data points and write them into the shared embeddings table. The original transcript is not embedded directly. In our experiments, accuracy increased significantly when the thread was normalized into a consistent format.(7,9) The additional metadata also gives the semantic match more useful signal.

Bursting

At this point Slack search was good, but we kept encountering the same problem: important messages inside long threads were not always represented in the thread-level summary.

To boost the signal from individual messages, we use bursting. A burst is a run of consecutive messages from the same author. We embed individual bursts with the thread topic prepended as context(2) because sometimes the answer lives in one tangent message whose vocabulary never makes it into the thread summary. Burst embeddings make that message findable on its own.

To prevent low-signal data from reaching the database, each burst is scored against a weighted combination of signals and must clear a threshold before it is embedded:

It contains a relatively rare token across the corpus, with IDF of at least 4.0.
The combined burst is at least 200 characters.
One or more messages in the burst contain reactions, providing a social boost.
AUTHOR A - SHORT
AUTHOR A - FOLLOW-UP
AUTHOR B - TECHNICAL DETAIL
AUTHOR B - RESOLUTION
AUTHOR C - ACK
BURST 01 - FILTERED
BURST 02 - EMBEDDED
SHORT - COMMON TOKENS - NO REACTIONS
LONG - RARE TERMS - REACTED TO

After distillation, qualifying bursts are embedded and stored in the embeddings table alongside the thread-level record.

Code repositories

Initially we debated whether embedding code repositories was necessary. With the rise of Claude Code and other command-line tools, creating code embeddings felt counterintuitive when it seemed like “grep is all you need.” After talking with others in the industry and reading Cursor’s findings on semantic search in large codebases, we decided to try.

We have many internal repositories, some larger than 40 GB. Our main concern was how to keep them current efficiently.

Using CocoIndex to maintain code embeddings

After several experiments, we landed on CocoIndex, an open-source document embedding framework that specializes in vectorizing codebases.

For each repository, we split the code using language-specific regex boundaries ordered from coarse to fine. The splitter tries higher-level boundaries, such as classes, first. If a resulting chunk is still too large, it falls back to method boundaries and then smaller blocks. We embed the resulting chunks and write the vectors to Postgres. A single file may generate multiple embeddings at different levels of specificity, such as file-level and function-level records.

class CheckpointLoader {
 public:
  Status LoadManifest(Path p) {
    auto bytes = fs_.Read(p);
    if (!bytes.ok()) return bytes.status();
    manifest_ = ParseManifest(*bytes);
    return ValidateShards(manifest_);
  }
  Status WarmShardCache() {
    for (const auto& shard : manifest_.shards()) {
      cache_.Pin(shard.key());
      stats_.Record(shard.bytes());
    }
    return OkStatus();
  }
  Status Restore(RestoreOptions opts) {
    auto lease = coordinator_.Acquire(opts.cluster);
    if (!lease.ok()) return lease.status();
    for (auto id : manifest_.ordered_ids()) {
      RETURN_IF_ERROR(fetcher_.Fetch(id));
    }
    return coordinator_.Release(*lease);
  }
 private:
  FileSystem fs_;
  Manifest manifest_;
  ShardCache cache_;
};

CocoIndex tracks synchronization metadata in Postgres. On each commit, it re-embeds and re-exports only the changed code chunks instead of recomputing the whole repository. This worked especially well for us because the synchronization state and embedding store live in the same database.

As the number of codebases grew, we moved repository onboarding into configuration files that teams can submit themselves, including allowlists and denylists at the file-path level.

Custom data sources

Some teams already had their own databases and did not want to move data into Slack or a document system just to participate in the knowledge base. They wanted the same query surface over their existing tables.

To support this, we treat custom sources as plugin scripts. A team opens a pull request with a small Python module that knows how to read from its system and emit rows shaped like our embeddings table, plus a matching data source entry.

As long as the script writes into the shared database using the same schema as every other embedding row, the rest of the stack works unchanged. The data becomes queryable alongside Slack, code, and documents, with no special handling elsewhere in the system.

Planning and tool fan-out

For every query, we first run a short planning pass where an LLM decides which tools and data sources are likely to matter. The main tools:

subsystem_index: per-file LLM summaries.
search: the unified vector pipeline across Slack, wiki, code, and other indexed sources, merged and reranked internally.
search_slack: direct Slack retrieval.
search_code: ripgrep over source repositories.
recent_prs: recent pull requests relevant to the question.
who_knows: people with demonstrated expertise on a topic.

The planner works over a compact description of what we have indexed: which projects exist, which sources are available in each project, and what each source is good at answering. Given the user’s query and active scope, it emits tool selections that the executor fans out in parallel, normalizes into a common evidence format, and passes to a final synthesis LLM.(4)

Reranking

A document can surface near the top simply because it shares vocabulary with the query while answering a different question. Before reranking, we combine the retrievers’ incompatible result lists with reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF. For every document, we add weight / (60 + rank) for each list in which it appears, with a default weight of 1.0 and a smoothing constant of 60.

The smoothing constant makes consensus matter more than a single strong vote: a document that shows up near the top across several retrievers can beat one that ranks first in only one of them. We then merge duplicate chunks back to one source, cap how many results each file can contribute, and end up with a more diverse top twenty.

We send the original query and those candidates to a small reranker model. It gives each document a score from zero to ten, and we keep the top ten.(6)

Once the ranking is final, we add context back to the winners. For example, if we match a wiki section we pull in the two neighboring sections so the heading, preconditions, and caveats that chunking split apart aren’t lost. This gives readers a complete snippet instead of a lonely paragraph that’s missing important context.

So the output of search is a rich packet of evidence: results fused from different retrievers, deduplicated at the source level, reranked against the actual question, and only then expanded with surrounding context.

MCP

In the MCP integration, we expose retrieval building blocks as direct tools instead of hiding them behind one “answer this question” endpoint. These tools are intentionally simple and as LLM-free as possible so clients can query them quickly and cheaply.(5)

Each MCP tool corresponds to one underlying retrieval primitive, such as search_slack, search_code, search, or who_knows. Tool inputs and outputs are narrow, structured, and stable, making them easy to call from any client or agent without embedding additional orchestration logic inside the tool itself.

Most tools run one query pipeline, such as vector search, lexical search, or ripgrep, apply lightweight scoring heuristics, and return raw evidence rows.

Claude Code, or any MCP-compatible agent, becomes the orchestration engine. It decides which tools to call, in what order, and how to assemble the results into a final answer or code edit. The retrieval layer itself does not depend on those LLM decisions in order to serve requests.

Web UI

In the web UI, the same tools exist, but they are connected to a complete query pipeline that runs end to end for every user question. The UI agent owns the planner and executor steps.

Planner: A lightweight LLM pass inspects the query and active project, then chooses which retrieval tools to invoke, such as search, search_slack, and subsystem_index.

Executor: The system fans those tool calls out in parallel, gathers the results, and normalizes them into a shared evidence schema with scores, recency, and source hints.

Synthesis: A final LLM pass takes the typed evidence bundle and original question, then produces the answer shown in the UI, including citations, caveats, and cross-source synthesis.

From the user’s perspective, the web UI is simply “ask a question and get an answer.” Under the hood, it runs the same planner → executor → synthesizer pattern that MCP clients can recreate explicitly.

WEB UI

Organization

As the corpus grew, “search everything everywhere” rapidly stopped being useful. Engineers on compiler teams did not want infrastructure runbooks in their results, and vice versa. Projects are how we make search relevant by default.

Projects and scoped search

We introduced projects as the primary way to organize the workspace that a query runs over. A project is a named bundle of data sources: specific Slack channels, code repositories, internal databases, and document spaces relevant to a team or initiative.

Projects are intentionally lightweight. The same data source, such as a shared incidents channel or central platform repository, can be referenced by multiple projects instead of being duplicated.

COMPILER PROJECT
PLATFORM PROJECT
COMPILER SLACK
MONOLITH REPO
SHARED INCIDENTS
PLATFORM REPO
CLOUD RUNBOOKS
DEFAULT QUERY SCOPE
DEFAULT QUERY SCOPE
Onboarding and defaults

During onboarding, users are prompted to select or create a default project that matches how they work, such as ML training infrastructure, Compiler, or Data Center Operations.

That default project is stored on the user profile and scopes queries automatically. A new engineer gets high-signal answers without first having to learn which Slack channels, repositories, or document spaces matter.

Final Thoughts

In the end, the knowledge base works because it meets people where the information already lives, instead of forcing everything into one rigid system. By combining various search techniques, we can surface evidence quickly. The result is a search experience that stays flexible enough for real company data, but structured enough to remain useful as Cerebras keeps growing.

With the rise of Claude Code and other command-line tools, creating code embeddings felt counterintuitive when it seemed like “grep is all you need.” After talking with others in the industry and reading Cursor’s findings on semantic search in large codebases, we decided to try.

blocks.text: After several experiments, we landed on CocoIndex, an open-source document embedding framework that specializes in vectorizing codebases.

blocks.text: For each repository, we split the code using language-specific regex boundaries ordered from coarse to fine. The splitter tries higher-level boundaries, such as classes, first. If a resulting chunk is still too large, it falls back to method boundaries and then smaller blocks. We embed the resulting chunks and write the vectors to Postgres. A single file may generate multiple embeddings at different levels of specificity, such as file-level and function-level records.

blocks.text: A document can surface near the top simply because it shares vocabulary with the query while answering a different question. Before reranking, we combine the retrievers’ incompatible result lists with reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF. For every document, we add weight / (60 + rank) for each list in which it appears, with a default weight of 1.0 and a smoothing constant of 60.

For every document, we add weight / (60 + rank) for each list in which it appears, with a default weight of 1.0 and a smoothing constant of 60.

blocks.text: The smoothing constant makes consensus matter more than a single strong vote: a document that shows up near the top across several retrievers can beat one that ranks first in only one of them. We then merge duplicate chunks back to one source, cap how many results each file can contribute, and end up with a more diverse top twenty.

blocks.text: Once the ranking is final, we add context back to the winners. For example, if we match a wiki section we pull in the two neighboring sections so the heading, preconditions, and caveats that chunking split apart aren’t lost. This gives readers a complete snippet instead of a lonely paragraph that’s missing important context.

blocks.html: MCP

blocks.text: In the MCP integration, we expose retrieval building blocks as direct tools instead of hiding them behind one “answer this question” endpoint. These tools are intentionally simple and as LLM-free as possible so clients can query them quickly and cheaply.(5)

blocks.text: Each MCP tool corresponds to one underlying retrieval primitive, such as search_slack, search_code, search, or who_knows. Tool inputs and outputs are narrow, structured, and stable, making them easy to call from any client or agent without embedding additional orchestration logic inside the tool itself.

blocks.text: Claude Code, or any MCP-compatible agent, becomes the orchestration engine. It decides which tools to call, in what order, and how to assemble the results into a final answer or code edit. The retrieval layer itself does not depend on those LLM decisions in order to serve requests.

blocks.text: Executor: The system fans those tool calls out in parallel, gathers the results, and normalizes them into a shared evidence schema with scores, recency, and source hints.

blocks.text: Synthesis: A final LLM pass takes the typed evidence bundle and original question, then produces the answer shown in the UI, including citations, caveats, and cross-source synthesis.

Jul 15 2026

How We Built Our Knowledge Base

Isaac TaiDaniel KimMike Gao

Employees ask our internal knowledge base more than 15,000 questions every day. It's become one of the most widely adopted internal tools at the company since launching 3 months ago. Used by humans, automations and agents.

At Cerebras, our teams work across data center operations, chip design, hardware, training, inference, cloud platform, and more. With hundreds of new employees joining every year, our communication channels were filling up with the same questions:

“Where can I find X?”
“Who is the expert in Y?”
“What is Z?”

We built Cerebras Knowledge to help people connect people and systems to useful information.

Meeting data where it lives

Finding information inside an organization is hard. The data is scattered across tools, and every quarter or so someone proposes the same brilliant fix: let’s record everything in one platform so that all information is in a single place. The dream of a single source of truth, of course, rarely works in practice.

Information is generated wherever it is convenient and ergonomic: suggested edits in a document, threads in Slack, code references in GitHub, and status metadata in Jira. These platforms are tailor-made for their specific domains, optimized through years of product engineering and analytics. Discussing a pull request in Google Docs would be a terrible experience.

So we set out to design a system that required minimal change to existing behavior. On the data collection side, this meant extracting data from each platform directly.

Anatomy of a knowledge base

Our knowledge base provides three things:

  1. A platform for collecting and storing internal data.
  2. A platform for querying that data.
  3. A layer that enforces authentication and authorization, with auditing and analytics.

At the core is a single Postgres table that holds embeddings, raw summaries, and metadata from many sources. The system continually ingests data from across the company and maintains a query-ready datastore.

We wanted a data interface that was simple but could work with most forms of data. We also wanted other developers at Cerebras to be able to build custom connectors. The result is deliberately simple: every source, from Slack threads to netlists, lands in the same embeddings table, and anything in that table is immediately queryable through the same interface:

Each data source defines what the data is, how to connect to it, and how often it should be fetched. Each resulting embedding row follows the same interface regardless of whether it came from Slack, a code repository, a document system, or a custom database.

Slack

Slack was the most important data source we needed to design for. It is where the most up-to-date engineering discussions happen across the company.

How we process unstructured Slack conversations

We initially tested whether simple embeddings over raw text performed well enough. We quickly realized that vector search alone was insufficient for matching all relevant data.

Slack messages present several challenges:

  • Information density varies enormously: “hey yeah sure mike” and a detailed kernel explanation are both messages.
  • Message lengths vary, and shorter messages frequently beat longer, more detailed messages in cosine similarity.
  • The meaning of a message often depends on the surrounding conversation.

We needed a hybrid approach. We built Slack ingestion so every thread is retrievable through several search techniques at once, where each technique makes up for the weaknesses of the others:

  • Full-text search catches the exact tokens that embeddings blur together: error strings, flag names, host names. When an engineer pastes a literal error message, an exact lexical match is almost always the best evidence, and no amount of semantic similarity should outrank it.
  • Embedding search catches paraphrase. The person asking “restore hangs after manifest load” and the person who answered “checkpoint stalls on the NFS mount” may never share vocabulary. Vector similarity is what connects a question to an answer written in different words.(1)
  • Inverse document frequency separates signal from filler. A short message built around rare tokens, such as an obscure config flag, deserves to rank. “sounds good, thanks!” sits close to many queries in embedding space but scores near zero once term rarity is taken into account.
  • Age decay encodes that Slack answers expire. Two threads can answer the same question, and the one from six months ago may describe infrastructure that no longer exists. When relevance is otherwise equal, the newer thread wins.
SEARCH / SLACK CANDIDATES FULL-TEXT
QUERY

“restore hangs after manifest load”

  1. 2W AGO
    NO SHARED TOKENS PARAPHRASE MATCH CKPT_PREFETCH: RARE RECENT WINS TIE
    Thread

    Checkpoint stalls on the NFS mount — set CKPT_PREFETCH=4.

  2. 1D AGO
    EXACT TOKENS ERR_MANIFEST_TIMEOUT: RARE
    Message

    ERR_MANIFEST_TIMEOUT: restore hangs after manifest load.

  3. 3H AGO
    FALSE NEIGHBOR NO RARE TOKENS
    Message

    sounds good, thanks! will try that

  4. 8MO AGO
    ALSO MATCHES 8 MO: DECAYED
    Thread

    restore hangs after manifest load → use LEGACY_FETCHER=1.

BOOSTED BY THIS SIGNAL PENALIZED

No single scorer is trusted on its own. Each technique produces its own ranked view of the same corpus, and those views are fused at query time (see Reranking).

Socket Mode

To collect data in real time, we installed a Slack bot into our workspace and ran it in Socket Mode. Slack pushes every message event to us over a persistent WebSocket, so we get real-time updates without polling the Web API and burning through its rate limits.

When an event arrives, we immediately acknowledge it, deduplicate it using the stable event ID, and mark the message for the ingest consumer.

The ingest consumer does not save a new message in isolation. It resolves the thread that the message belongs to and re-fetches the entire conversation, including the parent and every reply, from the Slack API. It then writes the whole thread back as one row. A reply to an existing thread therefore re-pulls the parent and all siblings, so the stored content, participant list, and last-activity timestamp always reflect the complete conversation.

Every Slack channel in our system has its own data source. This provides fine-grained tuning for data freshness. A team may choose to ingest a busy incident channel more frequently, for example.

Threads and messages

Raw Slack text is keyword-searchable as soon as it lands because we maintain a Postgres full-text (GIN) index over the raw content. To enable useful vector search, however, we do some additional processing.(8)

During distillation, an LLM extracts structured data from the full thread:

  • A one-line question that an engineer would actually search for.
  • A short summary.
  • The resolution.
  • The systems and code references mentioned.
#CKPT-SUPPORT / THREAD_8F42 FULL THREAD INPUT
  1. 09:14
    QUESTION
    Maya

    Restore stalls after manifest load on the larger cluster. Small runs are fine.

  2. 09:17
    SUMMARY
    Owen

    I can reproduce with 128 shards. The logs stop before cache warmup.

  3. 09:18
    CONTEXT
    Sam

    My laptop also stalls when it sees Monday.

  4. 09:21
    RESOLUTION
    Maya

    Setting CKPT_PREFETCH=4 makes it complete. The default is too high for the NFS mount.

  5. VECTOR
    Pgvector

    READY One consistent record, 3,072 dimensions

DISTILL
FULL THREAD
STRUCTURED ARTIFACT ONE PER THREAD
{
"question" "Why does restore stall after manifest load?"
"summary" "Large restores stop before cache warmup."
"resolution" "Set CKPT_PREFETCH=4 for the NFS mount."
"systems" ["checkpoint restore", "NFS"]
"code_refs" ["CKPT_PREFETCH"]
}
EXTRACTED FROM ALL FOUR MESSAGES
NORMALIZE
+ EMBED
EMBEDDING ROW PGVECTOR

Question + summary + resolution + systems + code references

sourceslack_thread
source_idthread_8f42
embedding3,072 dims

ONE QUERYABLE DATABASE RECORD

We embed these data points and write them into the shared embeddings table. The original transcript is not embedded directly. In our experiments, accuracy increased significantly when the thread was normalized into a consistent format.(7,9) The additional metadata also gives the semantic match more useful signal.

Bursting

At this point Slack search was good, but we kept encountering the same problem: important messages inside long threads were not always represented in the thread-level summary.

To boost the signal from individual messages, we use bursting. A burst is a run of consecutive messages from the same author. We embed individual bursts with the thread topic prepended as context(2) because sometimes the answer lives in one tangent message whose vocabulary never makes it into the thread summary. Burst embeddings make that message findable on its own.

To prevent low-signal data from reaching the database, each burst is scored against a weighted combination of signals and must clear a threshold before it is embedded:

  • It contains a relatively rare token across the corpus, with IDF of at least 4.0.
  • The combined burst is at least 200 characters.
  • One or more messages in the burst contain reactions, providing a social boost.

After distillation, qualifying bursts are embedded and stored in the embeddings table alongside the thread-level record.

Code repositories

Initially we debated whether embedding code repositories was necessary. With the rise of Claude Code and other command-line tools, creating code embeddings felt counterintuitive when it seemed like “grep is all you need.” After talking with others in the industry and reading Cursor’s findings on semantic search in large codebases, we decided to try.

We have many internal repositories, some larger than 40 GB. Our main concern was how to keep them current efficiently.

Using CocoIndex to maintain code embeddings

After several experiments, we landed on CocoIndex, an open-source document embedding framework that specializes in vectorizing codebases.

For each repository, we split the code using language-specific regex boundaries ordered from coarse to fine. The splitter tries higher-level boundaries, such as classes, first. If a resulting chunk is still too large, it falls back to method boundaries and then smaller blocks. We embed the resulting chunks and write the vectors to Postgres. A single file may generate multiple embeddings at different levels of specificity, such as file-level and function-level records.

CHECKPOINT_LOADER.CC LANGUAGE-AWARE
12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031
class CheckpointLoader { public: Status LoadManifest(Path p) { auto bytes = fs_.Read(p); if (!bytes.ok()) return bytes.status(); manifest_ = ParseManifest(*bytes); return ValidateShards(manifest_); } Status WarmShardCache() { for (const auto& shard : manifest_.shards()) { cache_.Pin(shard.key()); stats_.Record(shard.bytes()); } return OkStatus(); } Status Restore(RestoreOptions opts) { auto lease = coordinator_.Acquire(opts.cluster); if (!lease.ok()) return lease.status(); for (auto id : manifest_.ordered_ids()) { RETURN_IF_ERROR(fetcher_.Fetch(id)); } return coordinator_.Release(*lease); } private: FileSystem fs_; Manifest manifest_; ShardCache cache_;};

Language-aware recursive chunking selected

CocoIndex tracks synchronization metadata in Postgres. On each commit, it re-embeds and re-exports only the changed code chunks instead of recomputing the whole repository. This worked especially well for us because the synchronization state and embedding store live in the same database.

As the number of codebases grew, we moved repository onboarding into configuration files that teams can submit themselves, including allowlists and denylists at the file-path level.

Custom data sources

Some teams already had their own databases and did not want to move data into Slack or a document system just to participate in the knowledge base. They wanted the same query surface over their existing tables.

To support this, we treat custom sources as plugin scripts. A team opens a pull request with a small Python module that knows how to read from its system and emit rows shaped like our embeddings table, plus a matching data source entry.

As long as the script writes into the shared database using the same schema as every other embedding row, the rest of the stack works unchanged. The data becomes queryable alongside Slack, code, and documents, with no special handling elsewhere in the system.

Planning and tool fan-out

For every query, we first run a short planning pass where an LLM decides which tools and data sources are likely to matter. The main tools:

  • subsystem_index: per-file LLM summaries.
  • search: the unified vector pipeline across Slack, wiki, code, and other indexed sources, merged and reranked internally.
  • search_slack: direct Slack retrieval.
  • search_code: ripgrep over source repositories.
  • recent_prs: recent pull requests relevant to the question.
  • who_knows: people with demonstrated expertise on a topic.

The planner works over a compact description of what we have indexed: which projects exist, which sources are available in each project, and what each source is good at answering. Given the user’s query and active scope, it emits tool selections that the executor fans out in parallel, normalizes into a common evidence format, and passes to a final synthesis LLM.(4)

Reranking

A document can surface near the top simply because it shares vocabulary with the query while answering a different question. Before reranking, we combine the retrievers’ incompatible result lists with reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF. For every document, we add weight / (60 + rank) for each list in which it appears, with a default weight of 1.0 and a smoothing constant of 60.

The smoothing constant makes consensus matter more than a single strong vote: a document that shows up near the top across several retrievers can beat one that ranks first in only one of them. We then merge duplicate chunks back to one source, cap how many results each file can contribute, and end up with a more diverse top twenty.

We send the original query and those candidates to a small reranker model. It gives each document a score from zero to ten, and we keep the top ten.(6)

Once the ranking is final, we add context back to the winners. For example, if we match a wiki section we pull in the two neighboring sections so the heading, preconditions, and caveats that chunking split apart aren’t lost. This gives readers a complete snippet instead of a lonely paragraph that’s missing important context.

So the output of search is a rich packet of evidence: results fused from different retrievers, deduplicated at the source level, reranked against the actual question, and only then expanded with surrounding context.

MCP

In the MCP integration, we expose retrieval building blocks as direct tools instead of hiding them behind one “answer this question” endpoint. These tools are intentionally simple and as LLM-free as possible so clients can query them quickly and cheaply.(5)

Each MCP tool corresponds to one underlying retrieval primitive, such as search_slack, search_code, search, or who_knows. Tool inputs and outputs are narrow, structured, and stable, making them easy to call from any client or agent without embedding additional orchestration logic inside the tool itself.

Most tools run one query pipeline, such as vector search, lexical search, or ripgrep, apply lightweight scoring heuristics, and return raw evidence rows.

Claude Code, or any MCP-compatible agent, becomes the orchestration engine. It decides which tools to call, in what order, and how to assemble the results into a final answer or code edit. The retrieval layer itself does not depend on those LLM decisions in order to serve requests.

Web UI

In the web UI, the same tools exist, but they are connected to a complete query pipeline that runs end to end for every user question. The UI agent owns the planner and executor steps.

Planner: A lightweight LLM pass inspects the query and active project, then chooses which retrieval tools to invoke, such as search, search_slack, and subsystem_index.

Executor: The system fans those tool calls out in parallel, gathers the results, and normalizes them into a shared evidence schema with scores, recency, and source hints.

Synthesis: A final LLM pass takes the typed evidence bundle and original question, then produces the answer shown in the UI, including citations, caveats, and cross-source synthesis.

From the user’s perspective, the web UI is simply “ask a question and get an answer.” Under the hood, it runs the same planner → executor → synthesizer pattern that MCP clients can recreate explicitly.

Organization

As the corpus grew, “search everything everywhere” rapidly stopped being useful. Engineers on compiler teams did not want infrastructure runbooks in their results, and vice versa. Projects are how we make search relevant by default.

Projects and scoped search

We introduced projects as the primary way to organize the workspace that a query runs over. A project is a named bundle of data sources: specific Slack channels, code repositories, internal databases, and document spaces relevant to a team or initiative.

Projects are intentionally lightweight. The same data source, such as a shared incidents channel or central platform repository, can be referenced by multiple projects instead of being duplicated.

Onboarding and defaults

During onboarding, users are prompted to select or create a default project that matches how they work, such as ML training infrastructure, Compiler, or Data Center Operations.

That default project is stored on the user profile and scopes queries automatically. A new engineer gets high-signal answers without first having to learn which Slack channels, repositories, or document spaces matter.

Final Thoughts

In the end, the knowledge base works because it meets people where the information already lives, instead of forcing everything into one rigid system. By combining various search techniques, we can surface evidence quickly. The result is a search experience that stays flexible enough for real company data, but structured enough to remain useful as Cerebras keeps growing.

        var mid = (layers.length - 1) / 2;
        layers.forEach(function (layer, i) {
          var y = (p - 0.5) * (i - mid) * 14;

      }

      window.addEventListener('resize', rafThrottle(update));
      update();
      function rafThrottle(fn) {
        var queued = false;
        return function () {
          if (queued) return;
          queued = true;
          window.requestAnimationFrame(function () {
            queued = false;
            fn();

The data is scattered across tools, and every quarter or so someone proposes the same brilliant fix: let’s record everything in one platform so that all information is in a single place. The dream of a single source of truth, of course, rarely works in practice.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Information is generated wherever it is convenient and ergonomic: suggested edits in a document, threads in Slack, code references in GitHub, and status metadata in Jira. These platforms are tailor-made for their specific domains, optimized through years of product engineering and analytics. Discussing a pull request in Google Docs would be a terrible experience.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">So we set out to design a system that required minimal change to existing behavior. On the data collection side, this meant extracting data from each platform directly.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Anatomy of a knowledge base</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Our knowledge base provides three things:</p><ol class="list-decimal space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">A platform for collecting and storing internal data.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">A platform for querying that data.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">A layer that enforces authentication and authorization, with auditing and analytics.</li></ol><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">At the core is a single Postgres table that holds embeddings, raw summaries, and metadata from many sources. The system continually ingests data from across the company and maintains a query-ready datastore.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">We wanted a data interface that was simple but could work with most forms of data. We also wanted other developers at Cerebras to be able to build custom connectors. The result is deliberately simple: every source, from Slack threads to netlists, lands in the same embeddings table, and anything in that table is immediately queryable through the same interface:</p></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:5a81891aae75;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-002">

We quickly realized that vector search alone was insufficient for matching all relevant data.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Slack messages present several challenges:</p><ul class="list-disc space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">Information density varies enormously: “hey yeah sure mike” and a detailed kernel explanation are both messages.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">Message lengths vary, and shorter messages frequently beat longer, more detailed messages in cosine similarity.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">The meaning of a message often depends on the surrounding conversation.</li></ul><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">We needed a hybrid approach. We built Slack ingestion so every thread is retrievable through several search techniques at once, where each technique makes up for the weaknesses of the others:</p><ul class="list-disc space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><strong>Full-text search</strong> catches the exact tokens that embeddings blur together: error strings, flag names, host names. When an engineer pastes a literal error message, an exact lexical match is almost always the best evidence, and no amount of semantic similarity should outrank it.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><strong>Embedding search</strong> catches paraphrase. The person asking “restore hangs after manifest load” and the person who answered “checkpoint stalls on the NFS mount” may never share vocabulary. Vector similarity is what connects a question to an answer written in different words.(1)</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><strong>Inverse document frequency</strong> separates signal from filler. A short message built around rare tokens, such as an obscure config flag, deserves to rank. “sounds good, thanks!” sits close to many queries in embedding space but scores near zero once term rarity is taken into account.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><strong>Age decay</strong> encodes that Slack answers expire. Two threads can answer the same question, and the one from six months ago may describe infrastructure that no longer exists. When relevance is otherwise equal, the newer thread wins.</li></ul></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:edec91300fa9;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-hybrid">

      var root = scope.querySelector('[data-fig="hybrid"]');
      if (!root || root.dataset.initialized === 'true') return;
      root.dataset.initialized = 'true';

      const modes = [...root.querySelectorAll("button[data-stage]")]
      const label = root.querySelector("[data-mode-label]")
      const live = root.querySelector(".sr-only")
      const names = modes.map((mode) => mode.querySelector(".chunk-mode__title")?.textContent ?? "")

      modes.forEach((mode, index) => {
        mode.addEventListener("click", () => activate(index))
        mode.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
          if (!["ArrowRight", "ArrowLeft", "ArrowUp", "ArrowDown"].includes(event.key)) return
          event.preventDefault()
          const delta = ["ArrowRight", "ArrowDown"].includes(event.key) ? 1 : -1
          activate((index + delta + modes.length) % modes.length, true)
        })
      })

      function activate(index, focus = false) {
        root.dataset.stage = String(index)
        modes.forEach((mode, i) => {
          mode.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(i === index))
        })
        if (label) label.textContent = names[index]
        if (focus) modes[index].focus()
        if (live) live.textContent = `${names[index]} selected`

Each technique produces its own ranked view of the same corpus, and those views are fused at query time (see <a class="inline-link-article" href="https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base#reranking">Reranking</a>).</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Socket Mode</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">To collect data in real time, we installed a Slack bot into our workspace and ran it in Socket Mode. Slack pushes every message event to us over a persistent WebSocket, so we get real-time updates without polling the Web API and burning through its rate limits.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">When an event arrives, we immediately acknowledge it, deduplicate it using the stable event ID, and mark the message for the ingest consumer.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">The ingest consumer does not save a new message in isolation. It resolves the thread that the message belongs to and re-fetches the entire conversation, including the parent and every reply, from the Slack API. It then writes the whole thread back as one row. A reply to an existing thread therefore re-pulls the parent and all siblings, so the stored content, participant list, and last-activity timestamp always reflect the complete conversation.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Every Slack channel in our system has its own data source. This provides fine-grained tuning for data freshness. A team may choose to ingest a busy incident channel more frequently, for example.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Threads and messages</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Raw Slack text is keyword-searchable as soon as it lands because we maintain a Postgres full-text (GIN) index over the raw content. To enable useful vector search, however, we do some additional processing.(8)</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">During distillation, an LLM extracts structured data from the full thread:</p><ul class="list-disc space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">A one-line question that an engineer would actually search for.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">A short summary.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">The resolution.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">The systems and code references mentioned.</li></ul></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:ce52ab24863e;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-004">

The original transcript is not embedded directly. In our experiments, accuracy increased significantly when the thread was normalized into a consistent format.(7,9) The additional metadata also gives the semantic match more useful signal.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Bursting</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">At this point Slack search was good, but we kept encountering the same problem: important messages inside long threads were not always represented in the thread-level summary.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">To boost the signal from individual messages, we use bursting. A burst is a run of consecutive messages from the same author. We embed individual bursts with the thread topic prepended as context(2) because sometimes the answer lives in one tangent message whose vocabulary never makes it into the thread summary. Burst embeddings make that message findable on its own.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">To prevent low-signal data from reaching the database, each burst is scored against a weighted combination of signals and must clear a threshold before it is embedded:</p><ul class="list-disc space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">It contains a relatively rare token across the corpus, with IDF of at least 4.0.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">The combined burst is at least 200 characters.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside">One or more messages in the burst contain reactions, providing a social boost.</li></ul></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:75f84dd59cfd;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-005">

With the rise of Claude Code and other command-line tools, creating code embeddings felt counterintuitive when it seemed like “grep is all you need.” After talking with others in the industry and reading Cursor’s findings on semantic search in large codebases, we decided to try.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">We have many internal repositories, some larger than 40 GB. Our main concern was how to keep them current efficiently.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Using CocoIndex to maintain code embeddings</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">After several experiments, we landed on CocoIndex, an open-source document embedding framework that specializes in vectorizing codebases.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">For each repository, we split the code using language-specific regex boundaries ordered from coarse to fine. The splitter tries higher-level boundaries, such as classes, first. If a resulting chunk is still too large, it falls back to method boundaries and then smaller blocks. We embed the resulting chunks and write the vectors to Postgres. A single file may generate multiple embeddings at different levels of specificity, such as file-level and function-level records.</p></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:a2597858df29;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-006">

On each commit, it re-embeds and re-exports only the changed code chunks instead of recomputing the whole repository. This worked especially well for us because the synchronization state and embedding store live in the same database.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">As the number of codebases grew, we moved repository onboarding into configuration files that teams can submit themselves, including allowlists and denylists at the file-path level.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Custom data sources</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Some teams already had their own databases and did not want to move data into Slack or a document system just to participate in the knowledge base. They wanted the same query surface over their existing tables.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">To support this, we treat custom sources as plugin scripts. A team opens a pull request with a small Python module that knows how to read from its system and emit rows shaped like our embeddings table, plus a matching data source entry.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">As long as the script writes into the shared database using the same schema as every other embedding row, the rest of the stack works unchanged. The data becomes queryable alongside Slack, code, and documents, with no special handling elsewhere in the system.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Planning and tool fan-out</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">For every query, we first run a short planning pass where an LLM decides which tools and data sources are likely to matter. The main tools:</p><ul class="list-disc space-y-2 mb-4"><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">subsystem_index</span>: per-file LLM summaries.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">search</span>: the unified vector pipeline across Slack, wiki, code, and other indexed sources, merged and reranked internally.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">search_slack</span>: direct Slack retrieval.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">search_code</span>: ripgrep over source repositories.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">recent_prs</span>: recent pull requests relevant to the question.</li><li class="whitespace-pre-wrap ml-6 list-outside"><span class="text-accent">who_knows</span>: people with demonstrated expertise on a topic.</li></ul><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">The planner works over a compact description of what we have indexed: which projects exist, which sources are available in each project, and what each source is good at answering. Given the user’s query and active scope, it emits tool selections that the executor fans out in parallel, normalizes into a common evidence format, and passes to a final synthesis LLM.(4)</p></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:2eefa90269c2;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-007">

        col.innerHTML = '<button type="button" class="rrf-col__head" aria-pressed="true">' + label + '</button>';
        docs.forEach(function (doc) { col.append(card(doc[0], doc[1], id)); });
        cols.append(col);
        col.querySelector('button').addEventListener('click', function () {
          enabled.has(id) ? enabled.delete(id) : enabled.add(id);
          col.classList.toggle('is-off', !enabled.has(id));
          col.querySelector('button').setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(enabled.has(id)));
          renderMerged(true);
          live.textContent = 'Merged ranking updated';
        });
      });
      root.querySelector('.reset').addEventListener('click', function () {
        enabled.clear();
        lists.forEach(function (list) { enabled.add(list[0]); });
        Array.prototype.slice.call(root.querySelectorAll('.rrf-col')).forEach(function (col) {
          col.classList.remove('is-off');
          col.querySelector('button').setAttribute('aria-pressed', 'true');
        });
        renderMerged(true);
      });
      renderMerged(false);
      function card(doc, rank, list) {
        var el = document.createElement('div');
        el.className = 'rrf-card';
        el.dataset.doc = doc;
        el.dataset.list = list;
        el.innerHTML = '<span class="rrf-rank">' + rank + '</span><span>' + names[doc] + '</span>';
        return el;
      }
      function renderMerged(flip) {
        var before = new Map(Array.prototype.slice.call(merged.children).map(function (el) {
          return [el.dataset.doc, el.getBoundingClientRect()];
        }));
        var rows = score().slice(0, 6);
        merged.innerHTML = '<button type="button" class="rrf-col__head" tabindex="-1">MERGED</button>';
        rows.forEach(function (row, i) {
          var el = card(row.doc, i + 1, 'merged');
          el.classList.add('rrf-merged-card');
          el.tabIndex = 0;
          el.innerHTML = '<span class="rrf-rank">' + (i + 1) + '</span><span>' + names[row.doc] + '<br><span class="rrf-score">' + row.score.toFixed(4) + '</span></span>';
          el.title = row.parts.map(function (p) { return '1/(60+' + p.rank + ')'; }).join(' + ');
          el.addEventListener('mouseenter', function () { highlight(row.doc); });
          el.addEventListener('focus', function () { highlight(row.doc); });
          el.addEventListener('mouseleave', clear);
          el.addEventListener('blur', clear);
          merged.append(el);
        });
        if (flip) {
          Array.prototype.slice.call(merged.querySelectorAll('.rrf-card')).forEach(function (el) {
            var old = before.get(el.dataset.doc);
            if (!old) return;
            var now = el.getBoundingClientRect();
            el.style.transform = 'translateY(' + (old.top - now.top) + 'px)';
            window.requestAnimationFrame(function () { el.style.transform = ''; });
          });
        }
      }
      function score() {
        var totals = new Map();
        lists.forEach(function (list) {
          var id = list[0];
          var docs = list[2];
          if (!enabled.has(id)) return;
          docs.forEach(function (docPair) {
            var doc = docPair[0];
            var rank = docPair[1];
            var row = totals.get(doc) || { doc: doc, score: 0, parts: [] };
            row.score += 1 / (60 + rank);
            row.parts.push({ list: id, rank: rank });
            totals.set(doc, row);
          });
        });
        return Array.from(totals.values()).sort(function (a, b) {
          return b.score - a.score || names[a.doc].localeCompare(names[b.doc]);
        });
      }
      function highlight(doc) {
        clear();
        Array.prototype.slice.call(root.querySelectorAll('[data-doc="' + doc + '"]')).forEach(function (el) {
          el.classList.add(el.dataset.list === 'merged' ? 'is-target-hit' : 'is-source-hit');
        });
      }
      function clear() {
        Array.prototype.slice.call(root.querySelectorAll('.is-source-hit,.is-target-hit')).forEach(function (el) {
          el.classList.remove('is-source-hit', 'is-target-hit');
        });
      }
    })();
  </script>

We then merge duplicate chunks back to one source, cap how many results each file can contribute, and end up with a more diverse top twenty.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">We send the original query and those candidates to a small reranker model. It gives each document a score from zero to ten, and we keep the top ten.(6)</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Once the ranking is final, we add context back to the winners. For example, if we match a wiki section we pull in the two neighboring sections so the heading, preconditions, and caveats that chunking split apart aren’t lost. This gives readers a complete snippet instead of a lonely paragraph that’s missing important context.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">So the output of search is a rich packet of evidence: results fused from different retrievers, deduplicated at the source level, reranked against the actual question, and only then expanded with surrounding context.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">MCP</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">In the MCP integration, we expose retrieval building blocks as direct tools instead of hiding them behind one “answer this question” endpoint. These tools are intentionally simple and as LLM-free as possible so clients can query them quickly and cheaply.(5)</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Each MCP tool corresponds to one underlying retrieval primitive, such as <span class="text-accent">search_slack</span>, <span class="text-accent">search_code</span>, <span class="text-accent">search</span>, or <span class="text-accent">who_knows</span>. Tool inputs and outputs are narrow, structured, and stable, making them easy to call from any client or agent without embedding additional orchestration logic inside the tool itself.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Most tools run one query pipeline, such as vector search, lexical search, or ripgrep, apply lightweight scoring heuristics, and return raw evidence rows.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Claude Code, or any MCP-compatible agent, becomes the orchestration engine. It decides which tools to call, in what order, and how to assemble the results into a final answer or code edit. The retrieval layer itself does not depend on those LLM decisions in order to serve requests.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Web UI</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">In the web UI, the same tools exist, but they are connected to a complete query pipeline that runs end to end for every user question. The UI agent owns the planner and executor steps.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium"><strong>Planner:</strong> A lightweight LLM pass inspects the query and active project, then chooses which retrieval tools to invoke, such as <span class="text-accent">search</span>, <span class="text-accent">search_slack</span>, and <span class="text-accent">subsystem_index</span>.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium"><strong>Executor:</strong> The system fans those tool calls out in parallel, gathers the results, and normalizes them into a shared evidence schema with scores, recency, and source hints.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium"><strong>Synthesis:</strong> A final LLM pass takes the typed evidence bundle and original question, then produces the answer shown in the UI, including citations, caveats, and cross-source synthesis.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">From the user’s perspective, the web UI is simply “ask a question and get an answer.” Under the hood, it runs the same planner → executor → synthesizer pattern that MCP clients can recreate explicitly.</p></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" Engineers on compiler teams did not want infrastructure runbooks in their results, and vice versa. Projects are how we make search relevant by default.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Projects and scoped search</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">We introduced projects as the primary way to organize the workspace that a query runs over. A project is a named bundle of data sources: specific Slack channels, code repositories, internal databases, and document spaces relevant to a team or initiative.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">Projects are intentionally lightweight. The same data source, such as a shared incidents channel or central platform repository, can be referenced by multiple projects instead of being duplicated.</p></div></div></div><div class="col-[6/-1] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section data-slicetype="customFigure" class="relative bg-background text-foreground theme-light" data-sanity="id=d6088159-7525-4430-928f-3322c6e06b5b;type=blogPost;path=slices:2d911c01b376;base=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cerebras.ai"><div class="w-full h-full relative"><div class="mx-auto px-[2px]"><div class="mx-auto max-w-[1600px]"><div class="relative"><div class="grid-default"><div class="col-[1/2] h-full bg-background to-md:hidden"></div><div class="col-[1/-1] md:col-[2/6] relative px-pad grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-8 bg-background theme-light text-foreground"><div class="col-[1/-1] relative flex flex-col gap-4"><div><div class="cb-fig cb-fig-010">

A new engineer gets high-signal answers without first having to learn which Slack channels, repositories, or document spaces matter.</p><h3 class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[20px] md:text-[20px] leading-[1.3] -tracking-[0.02em] font-medium mb-4 mt-10">Final Thoughts</h3><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[16px] md:text-[16px] leading-[1.5] mb-4 font-medium">In the end, the knowledge base works because it meets people where the information already lives, instead of forcing everything into one rigid system. By combining various search techniques, we can surface evidence quickly. The result is a search experience that stays flexible enough for real company data, but structured enough to remain useful as Cerebras keeps growing.</p><p class="whitespace-pre-wrap text-[14px]
